notes.meaning: Paul tells the believers to copy his way of living, just as he copies Christ. He lived out what he taught, putting others first instead of seeking his own ease. We should only follow human leaders as far as they faithfully follow Jesus.

Paul praises the church for remembering his teachings and holding on to the instructions he passed on to them. These traditions were the basic rules and guidance the apostles gave for church life and worship. He commends what they did well before correcting what had gone wrong.

God has set up an orderly pattern of authority in creation and redemption. Christ is the head and leader of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God the Father is the head of Christ. Being under authority does not make a person less valuable, just as Christ is equal with the Father even while submitting to Him as Savior.

A man who prays or speaks God's word with a veil or head covering brings dishonor upon his head. In that culture, covering the head was a sign of subjection, whereas a man was called to reflect Christ's authority in the assembly. Praying uncovered showed that he looked up directly to Christ as his head.

A woman who prays or speaks God's message in church with her head uncovered brings shame on her head. Laying aside her head covering looked like rejecting her husband's leadership and the modesty expected of women. It was just as disgraceful in that society as having all her hair shaved off like an unfaithful woman.

If a woman refuses to wear a covering, she might as well cut her hair completely short. Since everyone agreed that a woman having her head shaved was shameful, she ought to keep her head covered in worship. Outward dress was meant to match the modesty and proper order given by God.

A man should not cover his head because he is made in God's image to reflect God's rule and majesty on earth. The woman reflects the honor and glory of the man, acting as his companion and partner. Her covered head shows respect for this order of authority.
In the beginning, God did not make the first man out of a woman. Instead, Eve was formed from the side of Adam. This order of creation shows why the man was given a position of leadership.

The first man was not created to serve as a helper for the woman. Rather, the woman was created to be a companion and helper suitable for the man. Her role was designed by God to complete him and share life together.

For this reason, a woman ought to wear a covering on her head as a symbol of authority and proper order. Paul adds that she should do this because of the angels. Heavenly angels watch over public worship and delight to see God's people showing reverence and proper order.

Even with this order of headship, men and women are not independent of each other in the Lord. Neither sex can get along without the other, and neither is higher in spiritual worth. In Christ's kingdom, they need each other as partners.

While the first woman was made from the man, every man since then is born of a woman through childbirth. Neither sex can boast of being independent. Above all, both man and woman receive their life and purpose from God.

Paul asks the Corinthians to use their own common sense and judgment. He asks whether it seems right and proper for a woman to pray to God in public with her head bare. Their everyday sense of decency would agree that she should be veiled.

The natural sense of propriety teaches that it is disgraceful for a man to wear long hair. Across most cultures, long or elaborately styled hair on a man looks soft and effeminate. Nature itself points out a clear difference between the two sexes.

A woman's long hair is given to her by God as a beautiful ornament and a natural covering. It suits her role and shows the natural dignity of womanhood. This natural veil points to why wearing a fabric covering in worship is fitting.

If anyone wants to argue about this issue, Paul says neither the apostles nor the other churches of God have any other custom. All the Christian assemblies followed this same practice of modest head coverings. A contentious spirit should not overturn what the whole church agreed upon.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe head coverings were a cultural practice for that ancient setting, so modern women need only maintain the timeless principles of modesty and respect without wearing a physical veil.
Some Reformed Christians hold that because Paul bases his instruction on creation, women in every generation are required to wear a head covering during public worship.

notes.meaning: Paul turns to a serious matter where he cannot offer any praise. Their church gatherings were doing more harm than good to their spiritual lives. When sacred meetings are handled badly, they harden hearts instead of building people up in faith and love.

Paul had received trustworthy reports that when the church assembled, they split into rival cliques and factions. These were not entirely separate churches yet, but unloving divisions within the same gathering. Paul found these reports easy to believe because of their selfish attitudes.

In this fallen world, God allows differences and factions to arise among church members. These trials act like a test to reveal who is genuine and approved in their faith and love. When some go astray, the sincerity of faithful believers shines all the more clearly.

Because of their selfishness and factions, their gatherings could not truly be called eating the Lord's Supper. They went through the outward motions, but their behavior destroyed the holy purpose of the meal. Christ designed it to be a shared feast of love, not a private party.

At their shared meals, each person rushed ahead to eat what they had brought without waiting for others. The wealthy brought plenty and drank until they were drunk, while poor members arrived to find nothing left and went away hungry. This selfish greed turned a holy feast into a shameful spectacle.

Paul asks if they do not have private homes for everyday eating and drinking. By turning the church gathering into a feast where poor believers were left with nothing, they were showing contempt for God's family and humiliating the poor. Paul strongly refuses to praise such disgraceful conduct.

Paul reminds them that he received the true pattern of the Lord's Supper directly from Jesus Himself and passed it on to them. It did not come from human invention. On the very night Jesus was betrayed by a close companion, He took bread into His hands.

Jesus gave thanks to God, broke the loaf, and gave it to His disciples, saying it was His body given on their behalf. He commanded them to continue this practice in remembrance of Him. The broken bread was an outward sign picturing His physical suffering and death on the cross for sinners.

differ.view: Baptists understand the bread to be strictly a symbol, so the Lord's Supper is a memorial meal that reminds believers of Jesus' sacrifice without His physical presence in the elements.
Lutherans teach that the true physical body and blood of Christ are really present in, with, and under the bread and wine.
Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach that Christ is spiritually present, and believers truly feed on Him by faith through the Holy Spirit rather than with their physical mouths.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach transubstantiation, the belief that the bread and wine completely change into the literal body and blood of Christ while keeping only the outward appearance of bread and wine.

notes.meaning: After the Passover supper, Jesus took the cup of wine and declared it to be the new covenant sealed in His blood. A covenant is a sacred agreement between God and His people, established by sacrifice. Each time believers drink the cup, they do so to remember His redeeming sacrifice.

Every time believers eat the bread and drink the cup, they preach and proclaim the Lord's death until His return. The Supper is a continuing testimony to the world that Christ died for sins and rose again. It looks forward to the day when He returns in glory and symbols will no longer be needed.

Anyone who partakes of the Lord's Supper in an irreverent or careless manner sins against the body and blood of the Lord. Paul is not talking about someone feeling personally unworthy, because all believers need mercy. He warns against treating the sacred symbols with mockery, division, or total lack of reverence.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics argue that being guilty of Christ's body and blood proves His actual presence in the sacrament, since one could not commit a direct crime against Christ's real body if the bread were merely an empty symbol.

notes.meaning: Before taking the bread and cup, each person should look closely at their own heart and life. Believers are called to test their motives, repent of sin, and approach the table with genuine faith in Christ. This self-examination is meant to help people take communion rightly, not to frighten them away.

differ.view: Lutherans practice close communion, admitting only those who have examined themselves and share the same confession of faith, so that the sacrament is received for their blessing and not their harm.

notes.meaning: A person who eats and drinks without recognizing the Lord's body brings divine judgment upon himself. This means failing to treat the sacred meal with respect, treating it like common food, or despising other believers who belong to Christ's body. The word for judgment here refers to God's discipline in this life, not eternal damnation.

Because of their irreverent and selfish behavior at the Lord's table, God had disciplined the Corinthian church. Many among them had become weak and sick, and some had even died. God sent these physical trials to wake them up to the seriousness of profaning His holy ordinance.

If believers would examine and correct themselves, they would not need to come under the Lord's judgment. Honestly confessing our sins and putting things right stops God from having to use painful discipline. Being strict with our own hearts spares us from His chastisement.

When the Lord judges His people, He is disciplining them as a loving Father rather than destroying them in wrath. This earthly chastisement is designed to correct and rescue them so they will not face final condemnation with the unbelieving world. God uses trouble now to keep His children safe for eternity.

Paul gives practical advice: when believers gather to eat the Lord's Supper, they should wait for one another. No one should grab their own food first or shut out others. The meal is meant to be a shared act of love and fellowship for the whole church family.

If anyone is so hungry that they cannot wait, they should eat their ordinary meal at home first. This prevents the church gathering from becoming a selfish feast that brings down God's judgment. Paul adds that he will give directions about any remaining details when he visits in person.
